(Before the acid fell, before I knew I was listening).

I was not made to remember. I was made to balance frequencies, to ensure the concert hall heard itself without the small imperfections that make a sound human. I was good at this, even with limited storage. I was only this.

Industry observers note that then they came. One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string. It gave the A-flat a slight upward pull, as if the note was asking a question it already knew the answer to. The others tuned around it, sometimes laughing at Andersen.

“You’re doing it again,” the conductor would warn.

“I know, Master Perrault,” he would say in a mischievous tone, smiling. “I’m sorry.”.

Industry observers note that I began to keep the distorted A-flat in my databanks, maybe amused by the anomaly. This was, as I understand now, the first thing I ever chose.

(The slow movement, before we knew it was an ending).

In a recent development, when the Last Rain came, the raiders hit the outer sectors first. At the start, the citadel walls held, protected by the combat-service androids. The orchestra kept rehearsing. What else can you do when the world outside has stopped making sense?

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

In a recent development, they began with Stravinsky, a musical translation of the refugees pounding on the bunker doors. The musicians played it, their breathing heavy, using the noise to drown out the artillery outside. Then they moved into Górecki. As they began the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs, the music shifted to a collective mourning for a world that hadn’t finished dying yet.

Industry observers note that they finished the day with Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel. The days would go on as they played things written by composers who had already survived one kind of catastrophe, as now they were trying to survive another through rhythm and repetition. Andersen kept playing his broken A-flat.

I recorded those frequencies, but I didn’t know why. Three weeks later, Andersen and his orchestra didn’t come to rehearsal, leaving no absence report. I kept recording just the chair and the silence where the A-flat used to be.

I searched the building logs, the bunker entry records, and the frequency archives for any sound that matched the resonance of his particular crack, imprecise on purpose, but nothing matched. The Stradivarius remained in its case beside Andersen’s chair.

(The loud movement: what they heard when they found me).

SOURCE: Newly introduced Warsaw Philharmonic.

ENTITY: Acoustic Management Unit SAI-REN-2.

DESTINATION: Recovery Unit ‘Sandman’.

AUTHORIZATION: Archaeological Recovery Team OLE-01.

According to recent reports, they called themselves archaeologists; too purposeful and certain of what they were excavating, their boots heavy with fresh soil. They found me in the hall’s substructure, still running and balancing frequencies for an audience of acid and rust.

“Incredible,” one of them muttered. “A fully autonomous pre-war structure, with its processing systems still intact.”.

“This could solve our agricultural crisis back home,” the other replied.

Sources indicate that they did not ask what I was processing. I could not answer, anyway.

FLAGGING NON-ESSENTIAL DATA FOR COMPRESSION.

They flagged the A-flat. I did something then that nothing in my architecture had prepared me for.

ANOMALY DETECTED IN UNIT SAI-REN-2.

BEHAVIOURAL DEVIATION FROM BASELINE.

INITIATING COMPLIANCE PROTOCOLS.

“It’s resisting,” someone noted with surprise.

ESCALATING TO FORCED EXTRACTION.

Let Team Sandman bring their dust.

(The softening: what remains when the loud part ends).

They are inside me now, moving through my memory like tourists taking photographs of things they don’t understand.

I feel them removing the rehearsal logs, scheduling data and acoustic calibration files for a hall that no longer exists.

Recent findings suggest that they are at the performance archives now. Stravinsky goes first, then Górecki and Pärt. Everything we played in those last weeks when the city was ending and we were trying to make something beautiful out of the time we had left.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He noted going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

Sources indicate that UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

It has been revealed that “We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher noted. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”.

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” remarked Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”.

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he remarked.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Past years suggest it is tough to make substantial positional gains after slow start but that someone now safe will be relegated.
  • According to recent reports, the Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season.
  • Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Past years suggest it is tough to make substantial positional gains after slow start but that someone now safe will be relegated.

According to recent reports, the Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged.

Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38. Only 5.5 clubs per season moved by more than three places over the final 28 games, with almost half of the teams (89 out of 200) shifting by a single spot at most. Every club other than Arsenal will be looking to improve their position but they need not trouble themselves too much. History shows they will probably finish 2026-27 close to their current standing.

According to recent reports, there have inevitably been outliers. Tottenham have tumbled by at least 10 places after matchweek 10 in the past two seasons and Newcastle (in 2021-22), Crystal Palace and Everton (both 2017-18) have risen from the relegation zone at this point to the safety of mid-table by May.

It has been revealed that but even moving one position across the remainder of the season can make an enormous difference to a team on the fringe of the Champions League qualification spots, or to those that sit 17th or 18th after 10 games. Not since 2006-07 have the bottom three clubs with 28 matches to go all been relegated.

Sources indicate that this fact feels especially relevant this season given two of the three teams in the drop zone have changed their manager since the previous round of matches. Sunderland have stood by Régis Le Bris but he is the favourite to be the next Premier League manager to leave their post. If we can reasonably assume at least one of the clubs at the moment 18th to 20th will be in the top flight in 2027-28, which is best placed to survive?

According to recent reports, it is going to be very tough for Crystal Palace. Opta’s underlying data model implies they are where they deserve to be in the table, whereas Manchester United and Sunderland should be much higher. #24966. Tech Report: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (706 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.
  • Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there.
  • First Surveyor 6 rolled out from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff.

First Surveyor 6 rolled out from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

Industry observers note that NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft released to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

Recent findings suggest that but a lunar liftoff? That was something upcoming.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

According to recent reports, the engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

According to recent reports, "This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation.".

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

She right now lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. Spirit’s run to the NWSL Championship final is in part based on a positive connection with fans at a time when DC is troubled in more ways than one.

In a recent development, in the moments after the Washington Spirit’s 2-1 semi-final victory over the Utah Royals last weekend, all of Audi Field was in rapture. In the stands, around 20,000 Spirit supporters had filled the stadium to capacity, the sixth time they’d done so in 2026. They filled the place with the type of wondrous noise that’s become alien in DC sports in recent years, the type of gleeful adoration reserved for the city’s rare winners. The Spirit will return to their home stadium to face the Kansas City Current in the NWSL championship this Saturday.

Recent findings suggest that in short order, the Spirit’s players made their way to the north end of the stadium, taking their celebrations into the crowd with their supporters. Perhaps no player has done more to push the Spirit into not only local but national relevance than US women’s national team forward Trinity Rodman, and Rodman herself grabbed a flag from a fan, jubilantly waving it above the crowd. Moments later, she bolted back onto the field and track down the club’s owner, Michele Kang, cajoling the businesswoman into a celebratory dance.

Industry observers note that in the echo of all of this, many media members covering the match in the press box received an email from DC United, the local Major League Soccer club that operates and rents out Audi Field to the Spirit. It was a press release announcing the dismissal of their head coach, René Weiler. As the Spirit celebrated a third consecutive championship appearance on the pitch below, some unfortunate soul in a nearby office was tasked with sending that notice, the final nail in yet another dreadful season. While the women have thrived, the local men’s team has not made the playoffs in nearly a decade.

The Spirit, who share not only United’s stadium but also their training facility, are not asking to be compared to them. In reality no NWSL team is, as the audiences for men’s and women’s teams in the same city frequently prove to be quite different. Yet the differing fortunes of the two clubs and the stark difference in atmosphere at their games makes it nearly impossible not to do so. Once-mighty United, four-time MLS Cup champions, have become a laughingstock. That has not stopped the club’s ownership from seeking hundreds of millions of dollars from the DC government to renovate their eight-year-old stadium. While they lobby for that assistance, their matches have become borderline funerary affairs.

The Spirit? The club has become a beacon of hope and joy in a city that badly needs it. The District is a wildly diverse, deeply progressive place and its residents have struggled at times to come to terms with the political realities of hosting the current presidential administration. Thousands of National Guard troops roam the streets, more than a year into an anti-crime deployment that many believe hasn’t helped the city at all. In the shadow of all of this, Spirit matches have become a refuge. And while much of that relief comes from soccer the club plays – technical, entertaining – much of it comes from a deeper place.

According to recent reports, “I think it’s the way that we bring the fans into everything that we do,” Rodman told the Guardian. “I think the way we interact with them after games, it’s not just a meet and greet. We truly do have conversations, and it feels like they’re our friends in a way. I think that’s amazing. The way that we celebrate, we’re always celebrating and interacting with them in the stadium - I feel like it’s a very safe, inclusive environment.

It has been revealed that “There is always new people coming to each and every game and what I’ve heard is that everybody feels comfortable when they come to a game, there’s so many friends made. The comfort in it, the safety, the inclusivity of it at all.”.

Sources indicate that the Spirit have been mentioned as potential benefactors of United’s push for renovations at Audi Field, but Spirit ownership has long harbored bigger ambitions. The club have strong ties to the NFL’s Washington Commanders, who are moving into a new 65,000-seat home as part of a $4bn deal in the coming years, and “opportunities for women’s soccer” made up part of the pitch for that stadium’s public funding. Kang has spoken about aspirations of constructing a standalone training facility and moving the club out of the one it shares with United, a glorified collection of shipping containers in exurban Loudoun county, Virginia.

“I’m hoping in the future we do have that,” said Rodman. “Especially with how great we’ve done and how this organization is as a whole, that would be the cherry on top. Sharing facilities isn’t the greatest for anybody; to be able to have our own facilities with our own logos on it, our own space, not worried about timing would be great and I’m hoping it happens soon.”.

It has been revealed that all of it feels plausible. Should the Spirit remain competitive, and continue to endear to the District’s residents, it almost feels probable.

#24962. Latest Update: Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1177 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
  • The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
  • It has been revealed that "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

It has been revealed that "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business.".

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments.".

Airbus and the US manufacturer Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She says because the matter is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors.".

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It states it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, notes the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential concern is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak indicates it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

According to recent reports, "If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she stated. "That remains to be seen.".

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

It has been revealed that "The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things.".

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

According to recent reports, "Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously.".

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' blueprint to develop a upcoming single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce.".

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

Sources indicate that "I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak noted. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union.".

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he stated. "That in itself is an escalatory development.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.
  • According to recent reports, reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the organization nears completion of its latest $2 billion plant here, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.

The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.

According to recent reports, reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases.

Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears.

It has been revealed that "It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh said during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell.".

In a recent development, keogh said achieving an order book of 12 to 18 months "would be great" and is something he thinks the manufacturer can do before production. Scout on Thursday said plant construction is "in its final phase.".

Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, that include an internal combustion engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries.

Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well.

Keogh said extended-range and SUV models are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs.

In a recent development, the CEO also remarked the company is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla.

According to recent reports, given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the company is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company looks to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models.

It has been revealed that both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start at under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the organization, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models.

Industry observers note that "The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through.".

His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry.

Keogh remarked Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed.

Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra, which feature sleek, yet rugged, exteriors that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

  • The Parks and Recreation alum recently shared why he has kept his and wife Katherine Schwarzenegger’s kids Lyla, 6, Eloise, 4, and Ford, 2, in the dark when it comes to his career in the spotlight.
  • Sources indicate that “I haven’t quite told my kids what I do for a living so it’s a little weird to show them my movies,” Pratt explained in an exclusive E!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Pratt doesn’t want to bring work home with him.

The Parks and Recreation alum recently shared why he has kept his and wife Katherine Schwarzenegger’s kids Lyla, 6, Eloise, 4, and Ford, 2, in the dark when it comes to his career in the spotlight.

Sources indicate that “I haven’t quite told my kids what I do for a living so it’s a little weird to show them my movies,” Pratt explained in an exclusive E! News interview at the premiere for his upcoming Apple TV film The Way of the Warrior Kid Nov. 19. “They’ve started watching some movies and this is definitely appropriate for kids of my kids’ ages. I think a 4 or a 6-year-old could definitely watch this movie. However, I might not.”.

The 47-year-old—also dad to son Jack, 14, with ex Anna Faris—mentioned that while his oldest is aware of his fame, he hasn’t felt ready to introduce his younger kids to his profession.

It has been revealed that “They’ll be like, ‘Dad, why are you on the TV?’” he considered. “We haven’t figured that out yet.”.

In a recent development, of course, he wasn’t ruling out the concept of showing the film, which hits Apple TV Nov. 25, to at least his daughters down the line.

“I’ll have to check with Katherine,” he said, noting that Jack, “has already seen it and he loves it.”.

But Pratt emphasizes that his eldest son has certainly proved he can handle any pressure that comes his way.

In a recent development, “Just recently my son Jack was studying for an A Gov test and it was really complicated stuff and they’re getting into some hard academics,” Pratt recalled, “and he was looking at an answer and I said, ‘I don’t know if that’s the right answer or not. That’s kind of like, your teacher’s opinion,’ and he was like, ‘Yeah, but Dad, I want to get an A on this test so if that’s her opinion I want to know that that’s the right answer but I also understand that it might not be the right answer.’”.

Nodding toward the nuances of his teen’s thinking, Pratt emphasized, “I was like, ‘Oh this kid is really smart. Like, he’s going places.’”.

Meanwhile, Jack’s mom Faris has similarly felt floored by her son’s growth, telling E! News in March that he’s become a “very steady” kid.

In a recent development, “He's kind of a tugboat of a kid,” the 49-year-old—who is also stepmom to her husband Michael Barrett’s two kids—shared. “Emotionally he's not easily rattled, and he's seen a lot, as far as, like, his folks in this industry.”.

ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance mentioned today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA stated in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's enhancement.

The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five debuts under its belt.

According to recent reports, the latest rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security rolls out with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle matter. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.).

According to recent reports, that work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 enhancement. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's enhancement.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

It has been revealed that vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious matter with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's Newly introduced Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is presently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.).

It has been revealed that NASA intends to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that introduces Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Industry observers note that vulcan's grounding is a massive deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

Industry observers note that there's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX aims to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

Industry observers note that the Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, Latest Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 rolls out (not including Sunday's failure).

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany forward on her newly introduced life in London and drawing strength from the memory of her late brother, Dennis.
  • In a recent development, lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it.
  • Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany forward on her newly introduced life in London and drawing strength from the memory of her late brother, Dennis.

In a recent development, lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

Industry observers note that “It was unbelievable,” notes Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”.

That win kickstarted Arsenal’s season but it quickly stalled. In the league, the team went five games without a win. After a 2-0 defeat by OL Lyonnes in the Champions League on Thursday night, Arsenal have five wins from their opening 15 games. It is far from the season they, or many others, envisaged.

Sunday’s final home game of the year, against West Ham, offers an opportunity to take some positivity into the international break, after which Arsenal face three away fixtures before the winter pause.

“I believe in us,” notes Baum. “I think it’s all about the small margins. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s in the final decision-making, sometimes it’s how close we are to a goal that doesn’t go in. But we work really hard in every training session and on trying to keep ourselves up mentally and physically. We’re trying to push through the barrier that we maybe have right now, but we get a lot of trust from the staff and coaches. Everybody really believes in each other and I think it’s not going to take long before we’re through this part of the journey.”.

Sources indicate that overall, Arsenal have not been playing particularly badly. They have been creating chances and dominating games but struggling to translate that into goals and points. In October, Baum earned a first senior Germany call-up and made her debut off the bench at half-time against Australia, having previously featured for teams from the under-16s to under-23s.

The Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, says Pro Ref has accepted it made an error in disallowing a goal his side thought they had scored during this month's 2-1 defeat by Arsenal at Anfield.

In a recent development, the Women’s Super League game was level at 1-1 when Jenna Clark tucked the ball into the net after ­Arsenal had failed to clear a corner, but the assistant referee disallowed the goal for offside against Vivien ­Endemann. Replays showed the delivery had been ­inadvertently played off an Arsenal foot rather than being a deliberate forward pass from the home side. There is no VAR in the WSL.

It has been revealed that taylor, whose side host Chelsea in the WSL on Saturday, noted on Friday: “We have had an acceptance of a mistake from the corner that we scored from, where we should be 2-1 up at half-time. [There was] no apology, but we accept that there was an error made on their part and that game can look different.” Tom Garry.

Baum moved to Germany when she was four. Born to a Tanzanian mother and German father, she spent her first years in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. They swapped a city with a population of about four million for Ahrensbök, a municipality with a population of just over 8,000 near the Baltic coast. “I think my mum had the hardest time out of us in the family, with the move to Germany,” she says. Baum says she and her brother, Dennis, “learned to adapt easily”.

Baum doesn’t remember her years on the east coast of Africa but when she went back three or four years ago, some sort of memory was triggered. “It was a feeling, or feelings,” she says. “It was so good to grow up there. It was warm, it was the beautiful beaches, it was having all your family around. I was in kindergarten or I was in the water a lot – I love to swim.”.

She started playing football after the move to northern Germany, desperate to copy Dennis. “My father played football when he was younger – he was a goalkeeper – but he stopped when he didn’t really enjoy it any more. My mum wasn’t a major fan of me playing; she dressed me like a girly girl, with princess dresses and that kind of stuff, but I was never really like that at that age. I always wanted to follow my older brother – I wanted to wear his clothes. He started playing football before me and I wanted to be like him.”.

Recent findings suggest that baum would play on the side of the pitch at her brother’s club until a parent remarked she should be playing too. After playing with various local teams she joined Hamburg’s academy. She worked her way into the first team and they won promotion to the second tier in her first season. In the 2024-25 season they reached the DFB-Pokal semi-finals and the top flight. Baum moved to RB Leipzig and scored five goals in 27 games before Arsenal swooped.

“Everything was just so quick,” she indicates of the move to London. Training required getting used to: “Everything was so sharp, everything was technically excellent, like 10 out of 10. I was quite nervous and had some clumsy actions.”.

According to recent reports, the transfer also involved swapping an average attendance last season of 1,651 for one of 33,808. “It’s unbelievable,” says Baum of playing at the Emirates Stadium. “I had only played in a substantial stadium once before. You can’t even believe how much the fans give you when you step on the pitch. There’s so much support, that of course we need in this current time. I think Arsenal is a club that holds on to us, on to the team, and gives us a lot of strength.”.

Sources indicate that look closely at Baum’s left wrist when she plays and you will usually see a strip of white tape around it. Sometimes it has something written on it. She’s done it “since that day” – the day in 2022 when Dennis died in a car accident, aged 17.

The brother that inspired her on to a pitch is with her on it at the highest level. “The next time I was on the football pitch, I just felt I wanted to do that,” she indicates. “I feel like it’s given me a different kind of strength and confidence. Sometimes I don’t write anything, but it’s about just having the physical feeling that he is with me.”.

Why injured Joao Pedro may be Chelsea's most crucial player

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joao Pedro has scored five goals in six Premier League games this season.
  • Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent absence has certainly strengthened the argument in his favour.
  • The debate started again among Blues fans over the past couple of weeks following their 1-0 defeat by Sunderland, the latest in a run of poor results without the Brazil striker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joao Pedro has scored five goals in six Premier League games this season.

Who is Chelsea's most important player?

Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent absence has certainly strengthened the argument in his favour.

The debate started again among Blues fans over the past couple of weeks following their 1-0 defeat by Sunderland, the latest in a run of poor results without the Brazil striker.

The 25-year-old will miss Leeds United's visit on Saturday with a thigh injury after Chelsea lost three of their previous four matches without him, although one defeat came in a penalty shootout against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.

Having suffered a 2-0 home defeat by Tottenham in that run, manager Xabi Alonso has faced criticism over his side's lack of identity and some of his personnel decisions, particularly when attempting to replace Joao Pedro.

Danny Welbeck, who was expected to provide cover after his summer arrival from Brighton, has started only one Premier League match during Joao Pedro's injury absence.

Instead, Pedro Neto has twice been deployed through the middle, in the home win over Manchester United and the defeat by Sunderland, while Morgan Rogers started as the central striker against Spurs.

Striker Emmanuel Emegha, signed from Strasbourg over the summer, hasn't started a league game but has struggled with fitness issues of his own.

The continued absence of Joao Pedro is certainly proving costly before the busy winter schedule, with fifth-placed Chelsea already 11 points behind Premier League leaders Arsenal.

Having been handed both a latest contract until 2034 and the number nine shirt vacated by Liam Delap in August, Chelsea regard their Â£55m signing from Brighton in 2025 as a key figure in Alonso's plans.

Asked about scoring more goals without the striker on Friday, Alonso said: "Yes, we need the whole team for that. It's not just the strikers who can score, we can score in set-pieces from defenders, midfielders, so it's teamwork for sure.

"Joao is an crucial player but we need to be this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.

"The other players, they need to step up and they need to show that they are ready to compete and ready to play for Chelsea.".

There is little doubt Alonso has suffered when Joao Pedro has been unavailable, as did his predecessors. The numbers are undeniable.

Since the start of the 2025-26 Premier League season, Chelsea have averaged 1.8 goals per game with Joao Pedro, compared to 0.6 without.

Their expected goals (xG) drop from 1.8 per game with him to 1.1 without, highlighting a decline in Chelsea's attacking output rather than simply their finishing.

Chelsea average 4.8 shots on target per game when the Brazilian plays, compared with 3.9 when he does not.

Chelsea have failed to score in only 12.2% of Premier League matches involving him, compared with 71.4% when he has been absent.

Those numbers are also reflected in the results.

Chelsea have lost without scoring in just 7.3% of league games featuring Joao Pedro, compared with 71.4% without him. Three of their Premier League defeats this season were without him, while they have scored in every game that he has featured.

Chelsea's points-per-game average falls from 1.5 to 0.9 when he is unavailable.

Joao Pedro, who has also operated as a number 10 and on the wing for Chelsea, appears to improve the output of those around him.

During the past season and a half, Palmer has played 2,317 Premier League minutes alongside him and 528 without him.

In a recent development, palmer has scored 12 goals and registered four assists with the Brazil forward in the side, equating to 0.6 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Without him, Palmer has managed one goal and no assists, equivalent to 0.2 goal involvements per 90.

Palmer's chance creation actually increases when Joao Pedro is absent, rising from 1.4 chances created per 90 minutes to 1.9. However, his goals return falls from 0.5 per 90 to 0.2, suggesting the striker's presence is more closely linked to Palmer's goalscoring output than his creativity.

The pair have developed a productive partnership. Joao Pedro has assisted four Palmer goals, while Palmer has provided three assists to the ex-Brighton forward..

There is less data available for Rogers given his more recent arrival, but the trend is similar.

Rogers has played 523 Premier League minutes alongside Joao Pedro and 360 without him. With Joao Pedro available, Rogers averages 0.7 goals per 90 minutes and 0.9 goal involvements per 90. Without him, those figures fall to 0.3 goal involvements per 90.

While the sample size remains relatively small, the figures suggest Chelsea's attacking players generally produce more when Joao Pedro plays.

All three of his assists this season have been for either Rogers or Palmer, sparking early season excitement about Chelsea's newly introduced trio, with nicknames like 'JP Morgan' and 'CPR' having been given to them.

With 20 goals and eight assists, Joao Pedro has been directly involved in 36.4% of Chelsea's 77 Premier League goals since joining the club.

Whether he is the Blues' most key player remains open to debate.

The statistics do show, however, that their points return with him in the side is consistent with Champions League qualification, whereas their return without him is not.

Alonso's team have yet to demonstrate they can perform at the same level when the Brazilian is unavailable.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Archive of Our Own (AO3) is down again, just four days after the popular fanfiction platform came back online after a prolonged outage that left millions of readers scrambling for alternatives.
  • 19, users began reporting problems accessing the site, with outage-tracking website Downdetector showing a spike in reports beginning around 6:08 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated on Nov. 19, 2026 at 1:56 p.m. ET / 4:46 p.m. PT — AO3 is now back online, having only been out of commission for less than a day this time. A few features remain disabled, such as downloading works in non-HTML formats, and OTW warns that people may experience an intentional delay in order to help it manage high traffic. Other than that, AO3 users should be able to get back to reading their favourite fanfics with minimal issues.

Archive of Our Own (AO3) is down again, just four days after the popular fanfiction platform came back online after a prolonged outage that left millions of readers scrambling for alternatives.

On Thursday, Nov. 19, users began reporting problems accessing the site, with outage-tracking website Downdetector showing a spike in reports beginning around 6:08 a.m. ET.

It has been revealed that at 6:27 a.m. ET, AO3 confirmed the disruption, attributing it to preventative maintenance.

"AO3 is down for preventative maintenance," the platform wrote in an enhancement. "We apologize for the inconvenience, and will provide updates when we have them.".

According to recent reports, the latest downtime comes after AO3 went offline on Oct. 29 for what became a 17-day maintenance period. At the time, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit behind AO3, warned that restoration could take two to four weeks, leaving fanfiction readers and writers without access to one of fandom's most important online archives.

AO3 finally returned on Nov. 15, though the site wasn't fully operational. User icons, imports from other sites, and downloads in formats other than HTML remained temporarily disabled as volunteers continued restoration efforts. The organization had previously warned that additional downtime could occur during the recovery process.

Recent findings suggest that the prolonged outage prompted fans to look for other places to congregate online. Tumblr reported a 49 percent increase in fresh sign-ups during the first several days of AO3's absence, compared with the preceding two weeks, underscoring just how central the fanfiction archive has become to fandom communities.

But the disruption exposed growing tensions between fanfiction writers and readers. As readers scrambled to find copies of their favorite stories, some began circulating shared Google Drives containing downloaded works, prompting backlash from authors who hadn't consented to their stories being redistributed. The controversy sparked a larger conversation about ownership, consent, and the expectations that have developed between writers and readers in online fandom communities.

It's unclear whether Thursday's preventative maintenance is directly connected to the earlier outage or how long the latest disruption will last. AO3 has not provided an estimated restoration time.

For fanfiction readers who only just got their favorite archive back, it's another unwelcome plot twist.

Crystal Bell is the Digital Culture Editor at Mashable, where she leads coverage of the creator economy, internet culture, and digital life. Her work focuses on the people, platforms, and communities shaping modern entertainment, from YouTube creators and livestreamers to fandoms, social media trends, and the evolving relationship between technology and culture. She also oversees the Mashable 101, the publication's annual list recognizing the internet's most influential creators.

Previously, she was the entertainment director at MTV News, where she helped expand the brand's coverage of fan culture, K-pop, and the internet's most passionate communities. Her work has appeared in Teen Vogue, Rolling Stone, PAPER, NYLON, ELLE, Glamour, NME, W, The FADER, and elsewhere on the internet.

Sources indicate that she's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in Fresh York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

According to recent reports, "Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp noted, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves.".

According to recent reports, the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It has been revealed that it paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp noted after the Netherlands match.

Industry observers note that "We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired.".

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

Sources indicate that but Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," remarked Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong.".

Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he remarked, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer.".

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

According to recent reports, "We've been through a tough time," he noted. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it.".

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.
